texto: More than any other pre-modern culture, the Romans are associated with feats of The Pantheon, the Colosseum, the Pont du Gard, monuments that seem to defy both gravity and time. But sometimes, even the Romans fell short of completing their most ambitious Today's video explores three of these unfinished

mega projects. Number three, moving the Tiber. Without the Tiber, Rome would never have The city emerged around a crossing of the river and was fed through the centuries of its apogee by grain barges towed upstream.

Almost every year, however, heavy rains caused the river to flood. About three dozen floods were severe enough to be recorded by ancient Cassius Dio, for example, records a flood that took place in 54 BC. The Tiber rose suddenly, flooding not only the low-lying parts of the city, but also many neighborhoods seldom The walls of the houses, being made of mud brick, soaked through and collapsed. Those who failed to seek higher ground were drowned in their rooms or were swept away on the current. Houses weakened by the flood continued to collapse for many days afterward. Such

damage was only the beginning. Major floods often destroyed docks and grain warehouses, causing widespread Whole streets of shops were ruined. Pools and puddles bred mosquitoes and Flooding seems to have grown worse over the centuries, possibly due to deforestation and erosion.

To end the Tiber's floods and the perennial problems caused by heavy barge traffic between Rome and Ostia, Julius Caesar proposed two plans for rerouting the Tiber. The more radical of these involved redirecting the river into a canal just below Rome. The canal would run through the Pontine Marshes, parallel to the coast, and finally reach the sea near Terracina, more than 60 km south. The more feasible of Caesar's plans

called for the Tiber to be directed around Rome. A diversionary channel would be opened just above the city, cut around the Vatican Hills, and returned to the original bed well downstream. By reducing the risk of floods, this scheme would have opened the low-lying plains along the Tiber for future Or so Caesar hoped. He was assassinated

before work could begin. Augustus settled for the less grandiose, but more practical solution of dredging the river channel. During the reign of Tiberius, yet another serious flood inspired a plan to reduce the Tiber's flow by diverting some of its tributaries. One tributary would be redirected north into the Arno. Another would be diffused by being split into many channels. Yet another would be dammed. Protests from towns near the affected rivers caused the Senate to reject the The Tiber continued to flood Rome until the modern embankments were built in the late 19th

century. Number two, Nero's Corinth Canal. Sailing east from Italy, Roman ships, which almost always hugged the coast, had a detour around the Peloponnese, the southernmost part of Greek peninsula. Besides adding days to the journey, rounding the Peloponnese was hazardous. Many vessels, including that carrying the Antikythera mechanism, were claimed by the shoals and storms of Cape Malea. The only way to

avoid rounding the Peloponnese was to cross the Isthmus of 6 km wide at its narrowest point and rising to a ridge nearly 100 m high, the Isthmus was bridged by the Diolkos, a grooved track that allowed ships, and more frequently loads of cargo, to be hauled from sea to sea by teams of oxen. The Diolkos could be used to transfer whole fleets. Marcus Antonius, grandfather of the triumvir, moved his ships over it in the first stages of a campaign against the Cilician pirates. Octavian did the same before Actium.

Hauling ships over the Isthmus on wheeled cradles, however, was time-consuming and difficult. And from the Greek Archaic period onward, plans for cutting a canal were Aside from the obvious difficulties of cutting through so much solid rock, ancient engineers believed that the sea was higher on the western side of the Any canal, they reasoned, would thus be filled with a roaring torrent of water that would flood half the Aegean.

Julius Caesar, never one for small plans, reportedly considered building a canal across the Isthmus. So did Caligula. Only Nero was megalomaniacal enough to actually begin the project. We'll discuss his disastrous attempt to do so after a brief word about this video's sponsor.

Returning to our topic, Nero personally inaugurated his Corinth Canal, filling the first basket of earth with a golden shovel. The actual digging was done by 6,000 Jewish prisoners of war under the direction of the emperor's engineers. 32 shafts, up to 40 m deep, were cut to inspect the nature of the rock along

the planned course of the Work began from both ends. On the eastern side, the workmen cut 1,300 m in from the coast. In places, the depth of the trench reached 30 m. On the western side, the cut reached 2 km inland. A third excavation was begun through the ridge at the center of the Isthmus.

Nero's death and the ensuing civil war stopped work on the canal. The project never resumed, became a byword for hubris. A dialogue attributed to the 2nd century sophist Lucian likened it to the failed canal that Alexander the Great had attempted to cut around Mount Mimas. Men, he opined, should not seek to alter what the gods have made.

Although the millionaire Herodes Atticus considered trying to complete the canal, no further work was done until the 19th Even then, despite the use of explosives and steam shovels, it took 12 years to finish the job. Since the modern canal followed the route of Nero's, virtually every trace left by the ancient workmen has been Number one,

a capital for Germania. Monuments to unrealized projects of conquest were scattered along the edges of the Roman world. At Inch Tuthel in Scotland, archaeologists discovered the remains of an unfinished legionary fort, demolished when the soldiers withdrew to the future line of Hadrian's Wall. 4,000 km away in the shadow of Mount Ararat, the ruins of a Roman style aqueduct bear witness to Trajan's short-lived annexation of Armenia.

Perhaps the most remarkable product of imperial overreach was built in what is now central Germany, about 100 km east of the Rhine. There, near the modern village of Waldgirmes, the Romans founded a city. Though protected by a timber palisade and at least two lines of ditches, this was a civilian settlement with no permanent garrison. The town at Waldgirmes, whose ancient name

we do not know, was laid out with a classic Roman grid of streets, graded to drain into central ditches. Along those streets were warehouses, taverns, and atrium-style houses, some with lead water pipes connected to the city aqueduct. Along with fragments of glass, pottery, and other goods imported from the distant Mediterranean, the excavators found fragments of a gilded equestrian statue of Augustus, which had been poised on a pedestal of Gallic stone at the center of the forum. Four other bronze statues, presumably honoring other members of the imperial family, stood beside it, facing a basilica and stoas with wooden columns.

Fragments of beams and planks preserved by the waterlogged soil allowed researchers to determine that the settlement at Waldgirmes was founded around 4 BC, shortly after Roman troops reached the Elbe. The city was abandoned little more than a decade later in the wake of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, when the inhabitants withdrew with legions back to the Rhine.
The buildings were burned. The head of Augustus's equestrian statue was thrown down a well until 1990, when it was accidentally rediscovered. Even the site of this unfinished Roman mega-project was
